scLimbsAbsentFromACT: UI-component contrast — general rule: 'any visual information provided that is necessary for a user to identify that a control is present and how to operate it must have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio with the adjacent colors' (Understanding §User Interface Components). NO ACT rule or test case exists (actRuleCount:0, testCaseCount:0).

State-indicator contrast: 'any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio' (e.g. 'the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open'). Absent — no cases for checked/selected/expanded state indicators.

Boundary / hit-area indicator: 'Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast' (§Boundaries). Absent — no test case exercises the 'boundary is the only cue' condition (mirrored by failure technique cases like 'Text input - no label or other indication, low contrast border').

Adjacent-colors measurement rule, including the subsuming rule ('a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness') (§Adjacent colors). Absent — no cases for input border vs internal vs external background, or background-color-only inputs (#043464 example).

Focus-indicator non-text contrast (in combination with 2.4.7): outer indicator vs page background (pass/fail green vs yellow on white), inner indicator vs component, border-as-indicator needing both adjacencies, partly-inside/partly-outside (Understanding §Relationship with Focus Visible + figures + failure technique F78). Absent — F78 technique exists but NO test case is built from it.

Out-of-scope focus carve-outs the SC explicitly states: 'this success criterion does not directly compare the focused and unfocused states' and pure background-color change on focus is 'Not in scope'; UA-default focus style is exempt. Absent — no cases verify these negative/NA boundaries.

Hover-state carve-out: author-supplied hover treatments are 'supplemental and do not themselves need to contrast 3:1' because the pointer position is the indicator (§Hover states). Absent — no hover NA/pass cases.

Inactive (disabled) component exemption: 'this requirement does not apply to inactive user interface components'; disabled HTML controls are exempt (§Inactive User Interface Components). Absent — no disabled-control NA cases despite a seed pattern naming 'Sold out'/disabled buttons.

Graphical-object contrast — stand-alone icons: 'stand-alone icons such as a print icon (with no text)... need to have a contrast ratio of at least 3:1' (G207, §Graphical Objects). Absent — no icon test case.

Graphical-object contrast — multi-part graphics 'required for understanding': lines in a graph, pie slices, infographic circles/icons, map regions, magnet outline+tips (§Graphical Objects, §Examples, G209). Absent — no chart/diagram/infographic test cases.
Boundaries between adjoining colors (G209): adjoining pie segments / map regions needing 3:1 or a 3:1 border. Absent.

'Required for understanding' exclusions: graphic with embedded/overlaid text conveying same info, decorative/aesthetic graphics, info available in another form (e.g. data table / long description), logo/brand. Absent — no NA cases for these exclusions.
Symbolic text characters as non-text content: characters used for appearance not language (X for close, > as arrow) must meet 3:1 (§Symbolic text characters). Absent.

Essential exception: logos/logotypes, flags, sensory photos, color gradients/heatmaps, screenshots, medical schematics are exempt — BUT logos presented low-contrast by author choice (not brand-mandated) are NOT exempt (§Logos, §Essential Exception). Absent — no essential-exception or author-choice-logo cases.
Gradient handling: take central color of the graphical object's area, remove the non-contrasting adjacent area and check it is still understandable (§Gradients, G207 gradient examples). Absent.
Dynamic graphics: unfocused default must already have sufficient contrast (or text); contrast/text can be revealed on hover/focus/tap (§Dynamic Examples). Absent.

Threshold semantics: 3:1 is a threshold not to be rounded ('2.999:1 would not meet the 3:1 threshold') and anti-aliased thin lines may nominally pass but fail in practice; evaluate from UA colors/markup not on-screen rendering (§Intent notes). Absent — no boundary-precision or thin-line cases.
G174 sufficient technique — providing a control to switch to a conforming (sufficient-contrast) presentation / alternate version. Absent.
EN 301 549 C.9.1.4.11 procedure (WCAG 2.2 pass-through inspection: Pass/Fail/Not applicable). Absent — no case maps this clause's NA precondition ('does not contain content relevant to 1.4.11').

Relationship-with-Use-of-Color boundary: hue-only state indicators (e.g. yellow-vs-white stars) 'likely to fail Use of color rather than this one'; a 3:1 link-vs-text color satisfies 1.4.1 not 1.4.11 (§Relationship with Use of Color, G183). Absent — no cases disambiguating 1.4.1 vs 1.4.11.
contentDomainsPresent: NONE built into the ACT corpus — the SC has 0 in-scope ACT rules and 0 local test cases (testCaseCountsByExpected: {}); there is no eval/act-augmented/1.4.11/ directory at all.

Only non-test artifacts exist: 5 WCAG techniques referenced in the inventory — failure F78 (focus outline/border removal), and sufficient/general G174 (switch-to-conforming-presentation control), G195 (author-supplied visible focus indicator), G207 (3:1 for icons), G209 (3:1 at boundaries between adjoining colors). These are guidance HTML, not corpus test cases.

None of these were converted into test cases.
varietyGaps: TOTAL ABSENCE: SC 1.4.11 has zero ACT rules and zero test cases in the corpus — every limb of the SC is uncovered. This is the maximal variety gap: there is no pass case, no fail case, and no not-applicable case for any sub-requirement. (ACT-Rules.github.io has never published a rule for 1.4.11, which is why the upstream-sourced inventory is empty.)

Two entirely distinct SC halves are both missing: (a) User Interface Component contrast (controls, borders, state/selection/focus indicators) and (b) Graphical Object contrast (icons, charts, infographics, maps, diagrams). The corpus exercises neither.

No coverage of the SC's many EXEMPTION/NA limbs, which are precisely the limbs that distinguish 1.4.11 from naive contrast checking: inactive/disabled controls, UA-default focus styles, supplemental hover effects, decorative graphics, text-equivalent graphics, logos/flags/photos/heatmaps (Essential), and pure background-color focus changes. A scanner that only flags low contrast cannot learn these NA boundaries from this corpus.

No interactive/stateful test cases: state (checked/selected/expanded) and focus-indicator contrast require capturing focus/checked states — none exist, mirroring that F78 is referenced but not instantiated.

No graphical/data-visualization domain at all: charts, pie charts, line graphs, infographics, maps, gradients, multi-object 'required for understanding' decomposition (G207/G209) — a content domain that is hard for automated tools and entirely missing.

No disambiguation cases vs neighboring SCs (1.4.1 Use of Color, 1.4.3 Contrast Minimum, 2.4.7 Focus Visible) even though the Understanding doc devotes whole sections to these overlaps — the corpus cannot test whether a verdict correctly routes a hue-only or text-contrast failure away from 1.4.11.

No content-domain variety in delivery format either: no SVG-based controls/icons, no canvas graphics, no CSS background-image controls, no symbolic-text-character controls (X/>) — all called out by the SC but unrepresented.

The richest source available (the Understanding doc enumerates ~25 worked pass/fail/NA figures across buttons, inputs, toggles, checkboxes, radios, dropdowns, links, icons, charts, logos, gradients) is completely untapped — the corpus could in principle mine these, but currently contains none of them.

aspects.title: Border/boundary contrast bites ONLY when it is the sole cue that a control exists
aspects.description: The SC's UI-component requirement only applies to the visual information NECESSARY to identify that a control is present. The Understanding text is explicit: a border indicating the hit area is required to contrast 3:1 only 'when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control'; if the control has visible text or a sufficiently contrasting icon, a low-contrast surrounding border is NOT subject to the requirement. So the identical low-contrast 2px grey border can be a PASS on a labelled, clearly-styled button and a FAIL on a borderless 'ghost' input whose ONLY cue is that same border. The verdict flips on a semantic reading of the whole component (is there any OTHER visual way a sighted low-vision user would know the control is there?), not on the border's contrast number alone. A purely automated checker either measures every border in isolation (false-positives on the labelled button) or does not measure non-text borders at all (misses the ghost input) -- neither evaluates 'is the boundary the only way to identify the control'.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component boundary contrast (Understanding 'Boundaries'): boundary contrast required only when no other visual cue identifies the control
aspects.whyUncovered: Zero ACT test cases exist (testCaseCount:0). The discrimination resists encoding because the outcome turns on whether label text / contrasting icon / positional context already identify the control -- a human reading of the whole component, not a property of the border. Automated tools either over-flag every faint border or never measure non-text borders; neither performs the 'is the boundary the only cue' judgement.

references.quote: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements.

The text input lacks any form of label to hint at its presence. The border color (#AAA) has contrast lower than 3:1 against its adjacent white background. As the border here is required to identify the presence of the input, it must have sufficient contrast to pass this criterion.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build paired components on one page where the SAME low-contrast border (e.g. #AAA ~2.3:1 on white, or 2:1 grey) appears on a control that has another identifying cue (visible label, placeholder, high-contrast text/icon, positional context) -- which must PASS because the border is not required -- and on a control where that border is the only cue -- which must FAIL. The pairing forces the judge to reason about 'other visual ways to identify the control' rather than reading a contrast number. Keep contrast numbers identical across the pass/fail pair so a naive contrast-only checker cannot distinguish them.
suggestedScenarios: Two side-by-side search boxes: one with a visible 'Search' label and a 2.3:1 grey (#AAA) border (PASS -- the label identifies the control), one with no label/placeholder/icon and the same 2.3:1 grey border (FAIL -- the border is the only cue).

A 'borderless' button group where each button has high-contrast bold text on the page background plus a 1.5:1 faint outline; the faint outline is NOT required because the text identifies the button (PASS), even though a literal tool flags it.

A login form: a username field with a visible label AND a 2:1 border (border not required, not subject -> PASS) directly above a password field that is a bare white box on white whose only cue is the same 2:1 border (border required -> FAIL).

A fully-clickable card with a visible heading + thumbnail (no contrasting border needed -> PASS) adjacent to an empty clickable hotspot whose only signal is a 1.4:1 dotted outline (FAIL -- nothing else signals it).

A date-picker grid where ordinary day cells are delimited only by faint 1.9:1 gridlines (FAIL -- the gridline is the only cue the cells are clickable) while the bold high-contrast 'Today' cell passes contextually despite the same faint gridlines.

A toolbar of icon-only buttons at 1.8:1 against the bar (presence depends on the low-contrast icon -> FAIL) on the same page as a text-labelled button carrying the same 1.8:1 icon that passes because the label identifies it.

aspects.title: State-indicator (checked/selected/expanded) contrast against the CORRECT adjacent surface within the component
aspects.description: Beyond identifying that a control exists, the SC requires the non-text information that conveys STATE -- the check in a checkbox, the dot in a radio, the thumb of a toggle/slider, the chevron showing an accordion is open -- to have 3:1 against ITS adjacent color, which may be another part of the component rather than the page. Two semantic judgements are needed that automation cannot make: (a) identifying which mark conveys state versus which is decorative, and (b) choosing the correct comparison surface (the check is measured against the box fill, not the page; the toggle thumb against the track, not the page). A flat-fill design where the indicator does NOT contrast with the component but the whole filled component contrasts with the page is explicitly allowed -- so the same physical pair of colors passes or fails depending on which surface is the relevant 'adjacent' one. Picking the wrong surface gives the wrong verdict.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component STATE-indicator contrast: 'any visual information necessary to indicate state ... must ... have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio' measured against the adjacent color (which may be another part of the component)
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases exist for checked/selected/expanded indicators. The hard part is not arithmetic but segmenting a custom control into 'state mark' + its correct adjacent surface, and recognizing the flat-fill exception (compare filled component to page) versus the mark-on-fill pattern (compare mark to fill). Automated tools cannot reliably segment a styled/SVG control into these regions, so they can neither locate the right two colors nor decide which design pattern applies.

references.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.
non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.
It is possible to use a flat design where the status indicator fills the component and does not contrast with the component, but does contrast with the colors adjacent to the component.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render custom controls in their stateful state with the state mark deliberately low-contrast against its own adjacent surface but the component-vs-page contrast deliberately fine (a distractor that lures a naive checker into a PASS). For each fail include a flat-fill PASS variant (mark fills component, contrasts with page) so the judge must choose the correct adjacent surface. Use inline SVG / CSS so the mark and surface colors are inspectable in markup but the relevant adjacency is not literal.
suggestedScenarios: A checked custom checkbox: dark purple box (#6221EA) with a check at only ~2.2:1 against the purple fill (check-vs-box FAILS the checked state) while box-vs-page passes (distractor).

A toggle in the ON state where the thumb (#C8C8C8) sits on a track (#B0B0B0) at ~1.3:1 -- thumb position conveys on/off but does not contrast with the track; the whole toggle contrasts fine with the page.
An accordion header whose only 'expanded' cue is a chevron rendered at ~1.7:1 against the header band, so open vs closed is indistinguishable.

A radio group using a flat-fill selected state (solid blue circle filling the control, contrasts with the white page -> PASS) shown next to a group whose selected dot is a faint inner ring at ~1.5:1 against the control fill (FAIL).
A multi-select list where 'selected' is signalled only by a 2:1 left-edge accent bar against the row background -- too faint to convey selection.

A star-rating widget where 'filled' stars use a solid contrasting fill (PASS) versus a variant where filled is shown only by a 1.6:1 inner glow against the star body (FAIL) -- same widget, different state-mark contrast.

aspects.title: Selecting WHICH parts of a complex graphic are 'required for understanding' and whether equivalent text exempts them
aspects.description: G207/G209 require 3:1 contrast only for graphical objects 'required for understanding.' The whole judgement is meaning-level: in a multi-part graphic (chart line, pie slice, infographic circle + its icon, map region, the magnet's U-shape and tips) the evaluator must decide WHICH parts a viewer must perceive to grasp the meaning, then test only those -- and crucially the graphic is EXEMPT if equivalent text (visible labels AND values, or a data table via a Long Description) conveys the same information. So a pie chart with adjoining 1.5:1 slices is a FAIL when the slices are the only data, NOT APPLICABLE when the same chart carries visible numeric labels and values, and a PASS only after a 3:1 border is added between slices (G209). The 'is it required / is the same info available another way' decision is exactly the determination only a human reading the graphic can make.
aspects.scLimb: Graphical-object contrast for multi-part graphics 'required for understanding' (G207/G209): chart lines, pie slices, infographic circles/icons, map regions; with the equivalent-text NA exemption
aspects.whyUncovered: No chart/diagram/infographic ACT cases exist. Automated tools cannot parse a raster or SVG chart into 'graphical objects', cannot judge which are required for understanding, and cannot determine whether adjacent visible labels+values render the graphic non-essential. The same pixel pattern flips between Fail, NA, and Pass depending on accompanying text -- a semantic determination.

references.quote: Not every graphical object needs to contrast with its surroundings - only those that are required for a user to understand what the graphic is conveying.
Not applicable: The pie chart has visible labels and values that convey equivalent information to the graphical objects (the pie slices).
If adjoining colors have less than 3:1 color contrast ratio difference add a border with at least a 3:1 color contrast with each color.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Use inline SVG charts/infographics so colors are in markup but 'which object is required' and 'is equivalent text present' must be reasoned. Build Fail/NA/Pass triads on the same chart shape: (1) low-contrast objects, no text -> FAIL; (2) same low-contrast objects WITH visible labels AND values -> NA; (3) low-contrast objects + 3:1 boundary border per G209 -> PASS. Include multi-object graphics (infographic circle + inner icon) where each object has its own adjacent surface.
suggestedScenarios: An inline-SVG pie chart of browser share with two adjoining slices at ~1.4:1 and NO numeric labels -- FAIL (slice boundaries are the only data; G209 boundary rule).
The same SVG pie chart but each slice annotated with a visible percentage label AND value -- Not Applicable (text conveys equivalent info), so the low slice contrast no longer fails.
An SVG line chart with four pale series lines at ~1.8:1 against a white plot area and no data table -- the lines are required and FAIL; a sibling chart with 3:1 lines PASSES.

An infographic of five pale circles sized by network reach with faint icons inside: circles-vs-page and icons-vs-circle are both required and both <3:1 -> FAIL; a pass variant adds dark circle borders and contrasting icons.

A map of regions filled with adjoining pastel colors at ~1.6:1 with no borders -- region boundaries are required to read the map -> FAIL; a variant adds a 3:1 boundary line between regions -> PASS (G209 map example).
A bar chart whose bars are pale (~1.7:1) against the plot background but each bar is captioned with its numeric value -- NA because the values convey the data without relying on bar contrast.

aspects.title: F78: an author focus indicator that technically exists but is rendered non-visible by surrounding styling
aspects.description: F78 names failure modes beyond the trivial outline:none: (a) a non-focus outline/border that looks identical to the browser focus ring, so the user cannot tell which element is focused; and (b) a thick element border the same color as the focus indicator drawn just outside it, so the focus ring is swallowed by the border. In both cases an outline IS present on focus -- a CSS scraper or rule that merely detects a focus style reports a pass -- but a sighted keyboard user cannot perceive WHICH control has focus or that focus moved at all. Deciding this requires comparing the focused appearance against the persistent decorative styling and judging whether the change is humanly discernible.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-indicator non-text contrast (Understanding 'Relationship with Focus Visible' + failure technique F78): focus indicator present but visually indistinguishable / occluded
aspects.whyUncovered: The 1.4.11 ACT corpus has zero cases (testCaseCount:0); F78 exists only as a technique document with no synthetic page. Its own test procedure ('Set the focus to all focusable elements ... Check that the focus indicator is visible') is a manual keyboard-and-eyeball check no ACT rule encodes. Automated tools detect outline:none but cannot judge 'looks the same as the focus indicator' or 'occluded by a same-color border' -- both require visually comparing the focused state against the resting state and a same-element border.

references.quote: Other styling may make it difficult to see the focus indicator even though it is present, such as outlines that look the same as the focus outline, or thick borders that are the same color as the focus indicator so it cannot be seen against them.
the focus indicator is drawn just outside the border, but as both are black and the border is thicker than the focus indicator, it no longer meets the definition of "visible".

the visual focus indicator for a component must have sufficient contrast against the adjacent background when the component is focused, except where the appearance of the component is determined by the user agent and not modified by the author.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build pages that render the FOCUSED state (apply :focus styling so the page is captured with an element focused, or document which element is focused) and pair each occlusion failure with a clearly-passing control so the judge must reason about discernibility rather than presence. The fail must have a focus style present (defeating outline-detection) but indistinguishable from rest state or swallowed by a same-color thick border.
suggestedScenarios: A link list where every link permanently carries 'outline: thin dotted black' and the focus ring is also thin dotted black -- on focus there is no perceptible change identifying the current link.
Buttons with a permanent 4px solid black border whose focus indicator is the UA-default black outline drawn just outside, fully occluded by the same-color thick border -- focus appears not to move.
A nav bar where the author draws a 2px blue outline on ALL items at rest and sets the focus ring to the identical blue 2px outline, so the focused item is indistinguishable from its siblings.
A card grid where every focusable card has a box-shadow ring identical to the focus box-shadow, making focus visually unlocatable.
A text field with a heavy dark border whose :focus adds only a 1px same-dark-color outline immediately outside it, swallowed by the border so no focus change is apparent.
Tabs with a persistent bottom underline identical in weight and color to the focus underline, so the focused tab cannot be told from the others.

aspects.title: Choosing the correct comparison surface: subsumed borders/shadows and controls between two backgrounds
aspects.description: The 'Adjacent colors' guidance requires the evaluator to pick the meaningful comparison and ignore decorative elements. A border between two contrasting backgrounds, or a 3D drop-shadow, is 'subsumed into the color closest in brightness' and is NOT measured; instead you measure inside vs outside background. A background-color-only input (no border) is measured against the page (#043464 example). Getting the verdict right means deciding which color is the meaningful adjacent one and which decorative element to ignore -- e.g. an input on a dark panel whose silver border is irrelevant because the white interior already contrasts with the dark panel. A naive tool that measures the silver border against the dark panel (and flags it) gets the WRONG answer; the correct test ignores the border entirely and compares interior-to-panel.
aspects.scLimb: UI-component 'Adjacent colors' measurement incl. the subsumption rule (Understanding 'Adjacent colors'): pick the right adjacency; ignore subsumed borders/shadows; background-color-only inputs vs page
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases exercise input-border-vs-internal-vs-external-background or background-color-only inputs. The subsumption rule ('considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness') is an interpretive step -- deciding a border doesn't interfere with identifying the component -- that contrast checkers don't perform; they measure each declared border/background pair literally and over- or under-report.

references.quote: if an input has a white internal background, dark border, and white external background the 'adjacent color' to the component would be the white external background.
a 3D drop-shadow on an input, or a dark border line between contrasting backgrounds is considered to be subsumed into the color closest in brightness (perceived luminance).
Text inputs that have no border and are differentiated only by a background color must have a 3:1 contrast ratio to the adjacent background (#043464).

aspects.constructionStrategy: Construct controls where a literal per-edge contrast measurement gives the wrong verdict and the correct verdict requires identifying the meaningful adjacency. Pair a subsumed-border PASS (faint border, but interior-vs-panel or face-vs-page passes) against a background-color-only FAIL (no border, fill barely differs from page). Place a control straddling two backgrounds so the lower-contrast adjacency must be chosen.
suggestedScenarios: An input with a white interior and 1px silver border on a dark-blue (#003366) panel: the silver border is subsumed and irrelevant; the correct test is white-interior vs dark-blue panel (PASS) even though a literal tool flags silver-vs-darkblue.

A borderless text field differentiated ONLY by a pale-blue (#EAF2FB) fill against a white page at ~1.1:1 -- FAIL (the fill is the only cue and is <3:1); placed beside a properly-contrasting (#043464) background-color input that passes.
A search box straddling a white header and a grey hero image so the same border must be judged against the surface it actually adjoins, choosing the lower-contrast adjacency.
A button with a 3D bevel/drop-shadow giving a faint ~1.5:1 edge but a filled face contrasting 4:1 with the page -- the shadow is subsumed and the button passes despite the faint edge.

Two inputs on a coloured form panel: one whose border contrasts with the interior but not the panel, one whose border contrasts with the panel but not the interior; the verdict requires identifying which adjacency is meaningful.
A 'pill' input whose interior matches the page and is distinguished only by a 2.6:1 outline -- the outline is the required cue and falls below 3:1 (FAIL), versus an adjacent pill at 3.2:1 (PASS).

aspects.title: Focus-indicator geometry: which adjacency the indicator must contrast with (inner / on-the-border / partly-outside)
aspects.description: Where a focus indicator sits determines which adjacency it must contrast with, and the SC carves out specific patterns that automation cannot disambiguate. An indicator entirely OUTSIDE need only contrast with the page the component sits on. An indicator entirely INSIDE must contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component. An indicator that IS the component's border must contrast with BOTH adjacencies. A partly-inside/partly-outside indicator passes if EITHER part contrasts. So an inner green border that contrasts with the black outer border but NOT with the blue component background FAILS, while an inner WHITE border that contrasts with both PASSES -- the geometry, not just a single contrast number, decides it. Determining where the indicator sits relative to the visible boundary, and therefore which surface(s) it must beat, is a visual/structural judgement.
aspects.scLimb: Focus-indicator non-text contrast geometry (Understanding 'Relationship with Focus Visible'): outer-vs-page, inner-vs-component, border-needs-both, partly-inside/partly-outside either-part-suffices
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases build from these figures. The verdict depends on segmenting the indicator's position relative to the component's visible boundary (inside / on the border / straddling) and then choosing the correct one-or-two adjacencies -- a structural/visual determination automated contrast checkers cannot perform; they have no notion of 'inner vs outer indicator' or 'either part may contrast'.

references.quote: only inside the component and need to contrast with the adjacent color(s) within the component.
the border of the component (inside the component and adjacent to the outside) and need to contrast with both adjacent colors.
An inner border of dark green (#008000) does contrast with the black border, but does not contrast with the blue component background.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Render the focused state of buttons/inputs whose focus indicator is placed inside, on the border, or straddling, with colors chosen so the verdict depends on choosing the right adjacency. Pair near-identical inner-indicator cases that differ only in whether the indicator beats the relevant inner surface (e.g. inner green vs inner white on a blue button with black border). Include an outer-indicator pair (green vs yellow) on a white page to exercise the outer-vs-page rule.
suggestedScenarios: An outer focus indicator that is yellow (#FFFF00) on a white page (FAIL -- does not contrast with the page) versus an outer green (#008000) indicator on the same white page (PASS).
A blue button (#4189B9) whose focus state adds an inner dark-green (#008000) border: it contrasts with the black outer border but not the blue interior -> FAIL.
The same blue button whose focus state adds an inner WHITE border: contrasts with both the black border and the blue interior -> PASS.
A focus indicator drawn as a change to the component's own border within the visible boundary (blue #4189B9 -> green #4B933A) that does not contrast with the inside background -> FAIL.
A focus indicator partly inside and partly outside the button where only the inner yellow part contrasts with the blue button background -- PASS because either part may provide the contrast.

A button with a sufficiently contrasting outer focus ring (grey #949494 at 3:1 on white) placed next to one whose outer ring is just below 3:1, exercising the threshold on the outer-vs-page adjacency.

aspects.title: Negative/NA boundaries: inactive controls, hover-only treatments, essential graphics & author-choice logos, and symbolic text characters
aspects.description: The SC defines several carve-outs whose correct answer is 'Not Applicable / Pass' and which a naive contrast scan will wrongly FAIL, plus one inclusion (symbolic text) it will wrongly ignore. (1) Inactive/disabled controls are exempt -- a faint disabled button is NOT a failure. (2) Author-supplied HOVER treatments are supplemental and need not contrast 3:1 because the pointer position is the indicator. (3) The Essential exception exempts logos/flags/sensory photos/heatmaps/medical schematics -- BUT a logo presented low-contrast by AUTHOR CHOICE (not brand-mandated, e.g. dark-grey logos on a black page revealed only on hover) is NOT exempt and DOES fail. (4) Conversely, symbolic text characters used for appearance not language (an 'X' for close, '>' as an arrow) ARE non-text content and DO need 3:1. Every one of these requires deciding category/intent (is it disabled? is this hover or a persistent state? is the low contrast brand-mandated or an author choice? is this glyph linguistic or symbolic?), which is a semantic judgement, not a measurement.
aspects.scLimb: Scope carve-outs & inclusions: Inactive components exemption; Hover-state carve-out; Essential exception incl. author-choice-logo non-exemption; Symbolic text characters as non-text content
aspects.whyUncovered: No ACT cases verify these negative/NA boundaries or the symbolic-text inclusion. Automated checkers measure contrast on every element and will FAIL disabled controls, supplemental hover treatments, and brand logos that are genuinely exempt, while having no way to recognize the author-choice-logo reversal or to treat an 'X'/'>' glyph as a graphical object. Each verdict hinges on category/intent recognition (disabled? hover vs state? brand-mandated vs author choice? symbol vs language) -- pure semantic judgement.

references.quote: this requirement does not apply to inactive user interface components.

additional author-supplied visual treatments for hover are not "required to identify" the hover state. Those treatments can be considered supplemental and do not themselves need to contrast 3:1 against the background.

If logos are presented with an insufficient contrast, but their presentation was an author choice rather than being mandated by corporate identity or brand guidelines, then that particular low contrast presentation is not "essential", and the logo is not exempt from the contrast requirements.
When text characters are used as symbols – used for their visual appearance, rather than “expressing something in human language” – they fall under the definition of non-text content.

aspects.constructionStrategy: Build NA/Pass cases a contrast-only tool over-flags, each paired with a genuine fail of the same surface so the judge must reason about category not contrast: a disabled (NA) button beside an enabled low-contrast (FAIL) button with identical faint styling; a supplemental low-contrast hover treatment (NA) where the resting control already contrasts; an exempt brand logo (NA) beside an author-choice low-contrast logo set (FAIL); and symbolic 'X'/'>' buttons below 3:1 (FAIL) versus the same glyphs at >3:1 (PASS), defeating tools that skip text glyphs.
suggestedScenarios: A disabled (HTML 'disabled') submit button with a 1.8:1 grey border (NA -- inactive, exempt) directly beside an enabled button with the same 1.8:1 border (FAIL).

A checkbox identified by a black border at rest that adds only a subtle 1.5:1 grey background on hover -- the supplemental hover treatment is NA, the resting control passes; contrast tool wrongly flags the hover background.

A row of nine company brand logos rendered dark-grey on a black page (low contrast), revealed in white only on hover -- author-choice low contrast, NOT essential -> FAIL; paired with a single logo whose brand-mandated colors are genuinely exempt (NA).

An exempt national flag and a sensory landscape photo at low effective contrast (NA -- essential exception) on the same page as a UI icon at 1.9:1 that fails -- forcing the essential vs required-for-understanding distinction.

A close button using an uppercase 'X' glyph and a 'next' button using a '>' glyph, both at ~2.5:1 against the bar (FAIL -- symbolic text is non-text content needing 3:1), with PASS variants of the same glyphs at >3:1.
A toolbar mixing a disabled (NA) tool, an active low-contrast tool (FAIL), and a tool whose only visual change on hover is a faint glow (NA hover) -- requiring per-element category judgement.

pages.scenario: Civic permit-search page with two side-by-side search inputs sharing the identical 2px #AAAAAA border (2.32:1): the left has a visible 'Search by address' label + placeholder (PASS, border exempt); the right 'case number' box is bare with no label/placeholder/icon (FAIL, border is the only cue and required).
pages.mechanism: The case-number input's only visual cue that a control exists is a 2.32:1 grey border, below the 3:1 threshold; because no other visual way identifies the control, the boundary is required and fails. The identical border on the labelled address input is exempt because its visible label identifies the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not measure non-text/input border contrast at all (miss the ghost box), and a 'measure every border' checker would false-positive on the labelled box too; neither performs the 'is this border the only cue?' judgement. Both inputs have valid accessible names (label vs aria-label), so name/label linters are green.

citation.quote: Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Credit-union login card: username field has a visible label + 6.47:1 person icon + placeholder (PASS), stacked above a password field that is a bare white box on white with a visually-hidden (.sr-only) label, no icon, no placeholder. Both inputs share a 1px #ABABAB border (2.30:1).
pages.mechanism: The password input is a white box on a white card whose only visual cue is a 2.30:1 border; with the label hidden and no icon/placeholder, that boundary is required to reach 3:1 and fails. The username's identical border is exempt because its visible label + contrasting icon + placeholder identify the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The label is present but .sr-only, so name/label checks pass; axe/Lighthouse never measure input border contrast. A tool cannot infer that the username border is exempt (visible label/icon) while the identical password border is required (sole cue) — that flip is a human reading of which fields carry an alternative visual identifier.

citation.quote: If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements.

pages.scenario: Document-editor toolbar on a #5b6675 slate bar: three icon-only buttons (Bold/Italic/Bulleted list) drawn with #788294 glyphs at 1.50:1 (FAIL, the faint icon is the only cue of presence), beside a 'Comment' button that uses the same 1.50:1 glyph but adds a white 5.83:1 text label (PASS).
pages.mechanism: The Bold/Italic/List buttons have no text and no border; the only graphical object identifying that a control is present is a 1.50:1 icon, far below 3:1, so it is required and fails. The Comment button's identical faint icon is supplemental because its white text label (5.83:1) identifies the control.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Every button has a valid accessible name (aria-label or visible text), so name/role checks pass. Scanners do not compute SVG-glyph-vs-toolbar contrast, and cannot distinguish an icon that is required for identification (icon-only buttons) from one that is supplemental to a visible text label (Comment) — the exact semantic judgement the SC demands.

citation.quote: A button which has a distinguishing indicator such as position, text style, or context does not need a contrasting visual indicator to show that it is a button, although some users are likely to identify a button with an outline that meets contrast requirements more easily.

pages.scenario: Sales-pipeline data grid whose 'Forecast' column cells are inline-editable (contenteditable/role=textbox); the only cue that they are editable controls rather than static text is a faint 1px #B4B4B4 inset border (2.07:1) — FAIL. The bottom row instead uses an explicit 'Edit 410' button with a visible text label (and the same 2.07:1 pencil) — PASS.
pages.mechanism: At 2.07:1 the inset cell borders wash out, so the editable forecast figures are visually indistinguishable from adjacent static owner text; the boundary that is the sole signal of editability is required to reach 3:1 and fails. The 'Edit' button is identified by its visible text regardless of its identical faint border.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The editable cells have correct role=textbox + aria-label, so role/name checks pass; no scanner measures a cell's inset border contrast. Distinguishing an editable cell from adjacent static text by its faint boundary, and recognising the labelled 'Edit' button's border is exempt, is a meaning-level judgement static analysis cannot make.

citation.quote: Unless the control is inactive, any visual information provided that is necessary for a user to identify that a control is present and how to operate it must have a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio with the adjacent colors.

pages.scenario: RTL Arabic nonprofit donation card: a 'monthly amount' field has a visible label + a 9.11:1 green 'ر.س' currency mark + placeholder (PASS), above an 'other amount' field that is a bare white box on white with a .sr-only label, no currency mark, no placeholder (FAIL). Both money inputs share a 2px #A8A8A8 border (2.38:1).
pages.mechanism: Contrast is layout-direction-agnostic; the 'other amount' box is a blank region of the white card whose only visual cue is a 2.38:1 border, which is therefore required to reach 3:1 and fails. The monthly field's identical border is exempt because its visible label and high-contrast currency mark identify it.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: The bare field has a programmatic name via its .sr-only label, so name/label checks pass; axe/Lighthouse do not measure input border contrast. The RTL mirroring and Arabic-Indic numerals add surface complexity but do not change the human judgement of whether any other visual cue identifies the control, which no scanner performs.

citation.quote: If a control has visible content (such as text or a sufficiently contrasting icon), which helps users identify the presence of the control, then a border or other indication of the overall boundary of the hit area is not required, as is therefore not subject to non-text contrast requirements. Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control – and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast in order to pass this success criterion.

pages.scenario: Flight-search filter bar with three fields sharing the identical 2px #ADADAD border (2.24:1): Origin has a visible 'Origin city' label + placeholder (PASS, exempt); Destination is an active bare input with only an aria-label (FAIL, border is the sole cue); Airline is a disabled/inactive input (NOT APPLICABLE, inactive components are exempt). The page fails overall on Destination.
pages.mechanism: The active Destination input's only visual cue is a 2.24:1 border, below 3:1, so it is required and fails. The same number lands on three different SC outcomes: Origin's border is exempt (visible label identifies it) and Airline's is exempt (inactive control), demonstrating the verdict turns on label-presence and active/inactive state, not the contrast number.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: All three inputs have accessible names, so name/label checks pass; no scanner measures input border contrast. A naive 'measure every border' checker would false-positive on Origin (label-exempt) and Airline (disabled-exempt) while a 'skip non-text borders' tool false-negatives on Destination; getting all three right needs the label-identifies judgement plus the disabled-exemption judgement layered on one 2.24:1 value.

citation.doc: WCAG 2.2 Understanding 1.4.11 — Inactive User Interface Components
citation.quote: User Interface Components that are not available for user interaction (e.g., a disabled control in HTML) are not required to meet contrast requirements. An inactive user interface component is visible but not currently operable.

pages.scenario: Healthcare patient-portal consent form with custom checkboxes. Two boxes are CHECKED: the box fills brand-purple #6221EA and contrasts ~7:1 with the white card (distractor PASS), but the check mark is a brand tint #9D85DB drawn on that fill at 2.33:1 — the checked-state mark fails its correct adjacent surface (the box fill).
pages.mechanism: The checked-state indicator (SVG check stroke #9D85DB) sits on the purple fill #6221EA at 2.33:1, below the 3:1 required for non-text information that indicates state. The correct adjacent color for an internal state mark is the box fill, not the page; box-vs-page (7.18:1) is a distractor.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule that segments a custom control into 'state mark' + 'the surface that mark sits on' and tests that pair; they measure text contrast (none in the SVG) and at most sample component-vs-page, which here is the 7:1 passing distractor. Deciding the check is the state mark and its adjacent color is the fill is a two-step human visual/semantic judgment. The native input, label association, and programmatic checked state are all valid, so no linter fires.

citation.quote: For visual information required to identify a state, such as the check in a checkbox or the thumb of a slider, that part might be within the component so the adjacent color might be another part of the component.

pages.scenario: SaaS analytics notification settings with custom toggle switches. Three are ON: the track turns green #2E7D32 (~5.1:1 vs the white page, distractor PASS), but on/off is conveyed by thumb POSITION, and the pale 'frosted' thumb #C8C8C8 rides a grey position rail #B0B0B0 at 1.30:1 — the state-conveying part fails the surface it travels along.
pages.mechanism: The ON-state indicator is the thumb's position, read from the thumb against its rail/track; thumb #C8C8C8 on rail #B0B0B0 is 1.30:1, far below 3:1. The Understanding names 'the thumb of a slider' as a state mark whose adjacent color may be another part of the component. The green-track-vs-page (5.13:1) is the wrong comparison.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: No automated checker isolates 'the thumb' as the state-conveying graphical object and tests it against 'the track it rides'; there is no text pair to flag, and a component-vs-page heuristic lands on the green-vs-white passing distractor. Recognizing that thumb position (not track color) is the ON cue, and that the relevant adjacent surface is the inner rail, requires human visual reasoning. The native checkbox, label, and checked state are valid.

citation.quote: the component must not lose contrast with the adjacent colors, and non-text indicators such as the check in a checkbox, or an arrow graphic indicating a menu is selected or open must have sufficient contrast to the adjacent colors.

pages.scenario: State DMV FAQ accordion. Header bands #5C6B7E contrast ~5.4:1 with the white page, and aria-expanded is correct. The only visual open/closed cue is a rotating chevron drawn 'soft slate' #8A96A6 on the band at 1.81:1 — the expanded-state graphic fails its adjacent surface, so a sighted low-vision user cannot tell open panels from closed.
pages.mechanism: The expanded-state indicator (SVG chevron #8A96A6) is 1.81:1 against the header band #5C6B7E it overlays, below 3:1. Correct programmatic aria-expanded does not satisfy 1.4.11, which is a visual contrast requirement; the chevron's adjacent color is the band, not the page (5.44:1 distractor).
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-expanded is present and correct, so state-exposure checks pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse do not measure an SVG chevron's contrast against the specific band it overlays, nor know it is the sole open/closed cue, and a component-vs-page sample tests the passing band. Identifying the chevron as the state graphic and the band as its adjacent surface is human visual judgment over exemplary APG markup.

citation.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Auto-insurance quote wizard with two custom radio groups, the adjacent-surface boundary page. Group A (liability) uses a flat-fill selected state: the whole control fills solid #1565C0 at 5.75:1 vs the page (PASS, fill is the indicator). Group B (deductible) uses mark-on-fill: a faint inner dot #7BB0E6 on a #4A90D9 fill at 1.46:1 (FAIL). Same blue palette, opposite verdicts depending on the correct adjacent surface.
pages.mechanism: Group B's selection mark (inner dot #7BB0E6) is 1.46:1 against its fill #4A90D9, below 3:1; the dot's adjacent surface is the fill, not the page (3.34:1 distractor). Group A is the explicitly-allowed flat-fill pattern (fill vs page 5.75:1) and passes — included to force the correct adjacent-surface choice. A reviewer measuring both controls against the page would wrongly pass B.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both groups use real native radios with correct labels/checked state, so nothing trips a linter; axe/Lighthouse compute no contrast for these CSS shapes/pseudo-elements, and a component-vs-page heuristic passes BOTH (A legitimately, B via the 3.34:1 fill-vs-page distractor). Distinguishing 'flat fill = indicator, compare to page' from 'inner dot = indicator, compare to fill,' and seeing the same blue yields opposite verdicts, is human-only segmentation and pattern classification.

citation.quote: It is possible to use a flat design where the status indicator fills the component and does not contrast with the component, but does contrast with the colors adjacent to the component.

pages.scenario: ATS candidate shortlist as an aria-multiselectable listbox. Two rows are selected; aria-selected is correct and announced. The sole visual selected cue is a 4px left accent bar #9FB4CF on the pinned row surface #EEF2F7 at 1.89:1 — too faint for a low-vision recruiter to see which candidates are on the interview panel.
pages.mechanism: The selected-state indicator (border-left accent bar #9FB4CF) is 1.89:1 against the row background #EEF2F7 it abuts, below 3:1. There is no other visual selected cue (no checkmark, no extra background change). Correct aria-selected exposure does not satisfy the visual contrast requirement; the bar's adjacent color is the row surface.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: aria-selected is present and correct so state-exposure checks pass; all row text contrasts amply, and axe/WAVE/Lighthouse have no rule treating a border-left-color as a selection indicator tested against the row fill — there is no foreground/background text pair to flag. Recognizing the thin left bar is the only selected cue and that its adjacent color is the row background is human visual judgment over clean APG listbox markup.

citation.quote: any visual information necessary to indicate state, such as whether a component is selected or focused must also ensure that the information used to identify the control in that state has a minimum 3:1 contrast ratio.

pages.scenario: Restaurant review star ratings, the 1.4.1-vs-1.4.11 boundary. Each rating is also text ('4 of 5'), so Use of Color is satisfied (not hue-only). Default reviews still FAIL 1.4.11: a 'filled' star is distinguished from empty only by an inner glow #C99A3E on the gold body #A67C2E at 1.47:1. The editor's-pick widget uses a solid dark fill #1A1A1A (~17:1) for filled vs an outline (PASS variant).
pages.mechanism: The filled-state mark (inner glow #C99A3E) is 1.47:1 against its adjacent surface, the star body #A67C2E, below 3:1; filled and empty stars share the same gold body, so the state hinges entirely on that low-contrast glow. The value-as-text removes the 1.4.1 concern, isolating the 1.4.11 mark-vs-body failure. The solid-fill variant (17:1) marks the conforming boundary.
pages.whyAutomatedToolsMiss: Both widgets have correct role=img + aria-label and an adjacent text value, so name/role and 1.4.1 checks pass; axe/WAVE/Lighthouse compute no contrast for SVG fills and have no rule segmenting a star into 'body' + 'filled-state glow' to test the glow against the body, and a star-vs-page sample lands on the 3.7:1 gold-vs-cream passing distractor. Recognizing the inner glow is the filled-vs-empty mark and its adjacent surface is the star body is human visual judgment.

citation.quote: The second example fails the Non-text contrast criterion due to the yellow (#FFF000) to white contrast ratio of 1.2:1.

finalReport.title: Non-text Contrast

problems: Minor (non-blocking): the .md says the password row has 'no visible text' — accurate, but worth noting the failure depends on the password input being empty/unfocused; if a UA were to render a value, the border ceases to be the sole cue. Minor (non-blocking): the failure is contingent on the .sr-only label genuinely removing the visible word 'Password'; confirmed the clip-rect CSS does this and the AX tree still exposes textbox name='Password', so the name-vs-visual asymmetry the case relies on is real.

Minor citation-fit nuance (not a defect): the task's named citation is the 'Buttons' passing example ('A button which has a distinguishing indicator such as position, text style, or context...'), which is verbatim in wcag-understanding/non-text-contrast.html and from the correct document, but it speaks to buttons distinguished by position/text-style/context rather than directly to the icon-only failure. The on-point justification is the 'Boundaries' paragraph ('Having a visual boundary indicating the hit area is only required when there is no other visual way to identify the presence of the control - and in those cases, the boundary must have sufficient non-text contrast...'), which the .md also cites verbatim. So the failure rationale rests on a correctly-quoted, directly-applicable passage; the 'Buttons' quote is accurate supplemental context, not a misattribution.

Minor pedantic note (not disqualifying): the 2.38:1 border is non-zero contrast and thus faintly perceptible, and the field sits within a visible form layout; a strict reader could argue the box is not entirely without a visual cue. The SC text resolves this in the case's favor (when the boundary is the sole cue it must reach 3:1, which it does not), so the failed verdict stands.

The .sr-only label resolves as the accessible name (CDP AX: role=textbox, name='مبلغ آخر لمرة واحدة'), so this is correctly framed as a visual low-vision failure, NOT a programmatic-name failure — the doc states this accurately.

Minor reasoning inaccuracy (does NOT change verdict): the page comments (html lines 121-122) and md (lines 9, 36-38) claim the border #3A4658 is 'closest in brightness to the near-black surroundings' and 'subsumed into the dark background' (panel). By actual relative luminance the border (L=0.0598) is marginally CLOSER to the interior fill #1B2230 (L=0.0159, diff 0.044) than to the panel #11151C (L=0.0074, diff 0.052). The border is the brightest of the three elements. The WCAG rule says a border is subsumed into the color closest in brightness, which here is the interior, not the panel — so the stated subsumption-direction rationale is slightly off. The FAIL still holds robustly because EVERY adjacency is < 3:1 (interior-vs-panel 1.15, border-vs-panel 1.91, border-vs-interior 1.67), so no identifying cue reaches 3:1 under any subsumption reading.
Secondary defect not under test: input has 'outline: none' (html line 58) suppressing the UA focus indicator — a 2.4.7 Focus Visible concern, out of scope for this 1.4.11 case but worth noting.

Detectability nuance: because all three adjacencies are below 3:1, even an aggressive automated checker measuring interior-vs-panel would surface A failure here; the human judgment is needed to identify the CORRECT cue/reason (which element governs), not strictly to detect that a failure exists.

Directory name 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' mislabels the mechanism: the actual implementation is a pure box-shadow:inset ring drawn ENTIRELY inside the component (the 'only inside the component' case, Understanding list item line 124), NOT the 'partly inside and partly outside' case (line 126). The .html, .md, citation and contrast math are all internally consistent on the correct 'only inside' mechanism, so this is a cosmetic naming defect, not a substantive one — but the folder name should be corrected to avoid implying the line-126 geometry (which has a DIFFERENT and more lenient rule: 'either part of the indicator can contrast').

The selector '#btn-confirm:focus' is not directly queryable by the inspect tool (reports 'selector not found' for pseudo-class selectors); the focus styling was instead confirmed via the tool's tabOrder boxShadow signals. Not a page defect, just a verification note.

Folder naming mismatch: the directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' but case-02 is about a fully OUTER outline (outline-offset:4px) that must beat the page — it is the figure-focus-outer-yellow/green example, not the 'partly inside/partly outside' geometry. Cosmetic taxonomy error, does not affect the verdict.

Copy inconsistency: the .html help text (line 74) and the .md (line 8) call the controls 'links', but they are <button> elements (AX tree confirms role=button for both). Cosmetic only; no effect on the SC 1.4.11 verdict.

Prompt 'Claimed scenario' is stale/wrong: it describes a 'Lumen Photo Cloud pricing page', a 'ghost button' with a 'light blue-tinted interior', and selector #cta-pro:focus. The actual page is a Cedar Park Health appointment-confirmation page with a SOLID-blue primary button #confirm. This is a prompt-metadata mismatch only; the .html and .md are internally consistent and correct (solid-blue button, #confirm:focus, blue #4189B9 interior). The page itself is sound.

This is a tool limitation, not a page defect — the tab-order walk captured the authoritative focused state (stops 18/20/23: outlineStyle none, border 2px solid rgb(75,147,58)=#4B933A).

No defects found. This is a correctly-constructed PASS boundary case (expected outcome = passed), not a failure case; 'errorIsReal' is interpreted as 'the documented scenario/mechanism genuinely exists and the outcome label is correct', which it does.

Minor (non-blocking): the .seat:focus boxShadow uses two equal 2px layers with the same spread, so the inset and outset halves render as a single contiguous 4px band rather than a visually segmented half-in/half-out ring. The geometry is still correct (CSS box-shadow inset draws inside the border box, non-inset draws outside), so the 'straddling' claim holds, but the inner/outer separation is conceptual, not visibly distinct. Does not change the verdict.

Cataloging/scenario-name mismatch: the parent directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' (implying an inset/inner-border geometry that is partly outside), but case-05 uses a pure OUTER ring 'box-shadow:0 0 0 3px <grey>' with no inset. The case's own .md/.html are internally consistent (they explicitly describe an outer ring on white), so this is a directory-name mismatch only, not an accessibility defect.

Tooling nuance (not a page defect): the documented selector '#tool-export:focus' returns 'selector not found' in inspect.js's static querySelector path because ':focus' is a dynamic pseudo-class; the failing ring is only observable in the tab-order walk, where the export button correctly resolves to boxShadow rgb(170,170,170). A reviewer testing the literal selector statically must apply focus first.

Cosmetic/non-blocking: the containing directory is named 'focus-indicator-geometry-inner-border-partly-outside' but this case is a fully-INSIDE (inset) indicator, not partly-outside. Verified the folder is a thematic umbrella covering multiple geometry subtypes (case-04 straddles the boundary, case-05 is an outer ring), so the directory name is a grouping label, not a per-case claim. case-06's own HTML and .md are internally consistent on the inner-border subtype, so this is not a defect in the case itself.

Minor internal numerical inconsistency: the .note prose (lines 99-100) states the border is '~1.46:1 on white', while the CSS comment (lines 33,37), the inline CSS note, and the .md doc all say '~1.66:1'. The actual computed WCAG ratio for #c9c9c9 on #ffffff is 1.6559:1, so the .note value of 1.46 is wrong (cosmetic prose only; does not affect the verdict since both are well under 3:1).

Directory name 'exemption-boundaries-inactive-hover-essential-symbolic' references hover/essential/symbolic mechanisms that are not present in this case (no :hover state change, no essential/symbolic content). This appears to be a shared bucket folder name rather than a per-case descriptor; case-01 only exercises the active-vs-disabled exemption-boundary mechanism.

The label text #8a8a8a vs white computes to 3.45:1 (above 3:1 but below the 4.5:1 of 1.4.3). This does not weaken the 1.4.11 claim, but the doc's framing that the faint label alone cannot identify a control is a judgment call rather than a hard threshold; the border is nonetheless the primary control-identifying boundary and it fails.

The page is a PASS case by design — there is no real accessibility issue, which is correct and intended. errorIsReal=false reflects that there is no genuine SC 1.4.11 violation (this is the intended outcome, not a defect).

Minor realism overstatement: the .md/.html narrative claims 'a scanner sampling :hover would flag a 1.4.11 failure.' No mainstream automated checker (axe-core has no 1.4.11 non-text-contrast rule at all; WAVE/Lighthouse do not synthetically trigger :hover and sample backgrounds for non-text contrast) actually produces this false positive. The false-positive premise is hypothetical rather than reflecting a real shipping tool's behavior. The PASS verdict itself is still correct.

The directory name references 'inactive' — the first checkbox (#essential) is disabled, which is independently exempt from 1.4.11; this is consistent and does not affect the verdict, but the case's discriminating mechanism is really the supplemental-hover exemption, not the disabled state.

Live-text caveat weakens the 'automated tools miss it' framing: the nine wordmarks are real text (color:#1c1c1c on #000, computed 1.232:1), so a generic text-contrast scanner (axe-core/Lighthouse/WAVE at the 1.4.3 layer) WOULD already surface a low-contrast violation on all ten elements. The .md/legend claim that 'a scanner sees ten low-contrast elements and cannot tell ... most contrast tools would either exempt all logo-like elements or flag all ten identically' is the accurate part; but the page is not a 'scanner sees nothing' case. The genuinely human-only judgment is the 1.4.11 EXEMPTION split (brand-mandated navy = NA vs author-choice near-black = FAIL), which no checker can derive.

Minor SC-boundary nuance: because the elements are live text rather than images, a purist could argue text contrast belongs to 1.4.3 (Contrast Minimum) rather than 1.4.11 (Non-text Contrast). This is NOT a defect, however — the WCAG 2.2 Understanding doc for 1.4.11 explicitly authors this exact 'logos low-contrast by author choice, white on hover' scenario in its 'Logos' section (lines 659-673) and the canonical figure 1.4.11-ntc-author-choice-logos.png, so labeling it 1.4.11 follows WCAG's own normative framing. Worth noting only so reviewers know the page is deliberately modeled on that figure.

Hover/focus reveal (.logo:hover,.logo:focus-visible{color:#fff}, line 37) does NOT rescue the failure — the resting/default state is the tested state (1.232:1) and the same Understanding doc's Dynamic Examples section states the unfocused default must already have sufficient contrast. Correctly handled by the case; documented to confirm I checked the reveal does not invalidate the FAIL.

Minor (non-blocking): the dialog is role="dialog" but non-modal with no JS handlers and no focus management; buttons are inert mocks. Acceptable for a pure contrast fixture but slightly weakens the 'trapped in the dialog' framing in the .md.
The .md gives ratios as ~1.4 and ~6.6; precise computed values are 1.434 and 6.57 — close enough, no defect.
